## Lead judgment

### Intent
> Add a `Proves it:` line to `templates/brief.md` after `Done when:`. The brief parser and jbus's pre-launch checks accept it only when it names something outside the agent (a test or command, a metric, a dataset, an external judge, or the user). They refuse an empty line, the template text, and any proof by the crew, crewmate, reviewer, agent, self or model, with a one-line reason. Briefs without the line are grandfathered or refused without stranding an approved row. The change includes tests for every accepted and refused kind, plus updates to the home skill and docs.

### Reviewers
- Reviewer A: 7 findings
- Reviewer B: 6 findings
- Both readers independently found the same central defect: the "outside" patterns are checked first and are loose. They also agreed on the duplicated head loop, the test-only `Brief.proof`, the `<` template check and the two Done-when items that cannot be seen in the diff. Only A raised permanent grandfathering and the double gate.
- The two readers give different line numbers in `parse.py` for the same code. A puts `_OUTSIDE` at :31 and `proof()` at :126; B puts them at :133 and :190. I could not check this against the repo. The lines below use B's numbers and name each symbol, so the crewmate should find the code by name.

### Act on

```
error src/jbriefs/parse.py:133 `_OUTSIDE` matches bare keywords (any backticked span, "make sure", any "%", "judge", "self-test", "his word", "eval", "github") and `proof()` (:190) accepts on the first match without reading `_SELF`, so lines naming only the crewmate, reviewer, agent or model pass the launch gate; the refused-kinds rule of the Done-when list is not met, and REFUSED in tests/test_briefs.py:299 has no near-miss case that would catch it: tighten the patterns (a path, `test_\w+`, or a backticked known tool/command; `make <target>`; `%` beside a metric word; "the user" not "his ...") and add executing REFUSED cases for each example both readers gave (principle: none) (bucket: Act on)
warning src/jbus/dispatch.py:157 `proven()` passes every brief whose `Proves it:` line is missing, not only those queued before this change, so leaving the line out bypasses the new gate indefinitely and the requirement survives only as prose in the home skill and docs/jbus.md:85: grandfather by something the queue records (row `approved` time or `brief_sha` before a cut-off) and gate a missing line on rows approved after it (principle: none) (bucket: Act on)
```

Why these two:
- **The patterns.** Both readers found the same thing, and each gave a concrete line that passes, for example "the crewmate will make sure it works" or "the reviewer is 100% sure". This check is the only thing between such a line and `dispatch._ready` launching the brief, so the task's main refusal does not work.
- **Grandfathering.** The Done-when list asks that queued rows not be stranded. It does not ask for a permanent exemption. As written, the exemption is a self-report: the brief says it is old, and nothing checks that. Tying it to the approval time keeps approved rows moving and closes the bypass.

### Consider

```
info src/jbus/dispatch.py:332 `proven()` runs only when `designed()` passes, so a brief failing both raises two gates in sequence and costs the user two re-approvals; collect both faults into one gate keyed by the brief sha (principle: none) (bucket: Consider)
info src/jbriefs/parse.py:199 `proves_it` repeats `dispatch.designed`'s head-line loop, and `dispatch.proven` (:157) is a pass-through over it; one `head_line(text, label)` helper in `jbriefs.parse` and a `(kind, check)` tuple in `_ready` would remove both, but moving `designed` is outside this task's Where and its do-not-touch, so that part is for later (principle: none) (bucket: Consider)
info src/jbriefs/parse.py:166 `Brief.proof` and `Proof.said` have no reader in `src/`, only tests; drop them or show the field on the jbriefs page (principle: none) (bucket: Consider)
info src/jbriefs/parse.py:188 the template text is detected by a leading `<`, so the guide with its brackets removed passes as "a test" and a real `<= 50 ms p95` line is refused; compare with the template's own line or match `^<[^>]*>$` (principle: none) (bucket: Consider)
```

Tradeoffs:
- **The double gate** is real, but it only happens when a brief fails both checks. Folding both faults into one gate would be cheap if the crewmate is already in `_ready`.
- **The duplicated loop** costs maintenance, not correctness. Only part of the fix is in scope.
- **The unused accessors** add surface with no consumer. They are cheap to remove and do no harm if left.
- **The template check** is the narrow edge of the Done-when line "refuses the template's own text". A practical home could hit it, but it is cheap to make exact.

### Noted
- Noted: 1
- The Result's grandfather-or-refuse statement, and the run of one real queued brief through the launch check with the line printed (A7, B6). The diff cannot show either. They have to be checked against the brief's Result, not sent to the crewmate as a finding.

### Dismissed
- Dismissed: 0

### Agreement Map
The readers converged on everything they both covered. The strongest signal is that both readers rated the pattern looseness as the main defect, and both said separately that the tests only pin the accepting side of the precedence rule. I merged that test gap into the same finding because the fix is the same. A alone saw the two issues at the edges of the gate: the bypass when the line is missing and the double gate. B alone noticed the false refusal of a leading `<`. The disagreement on severity was small: B called the patterns critical and A called them a warning. I took B's rating, because this check is the only barrier before a launch.

# Lead judgment

### Intent
> Section 3 of the /deeper design. The home skill gets a step in its own brief writing, with its own copy of the four questions. The step runs for research, perf, analysis and outcome briefs. It maps answer 2 to `Read:` or the request's sources, answer 3 to the crew's brief, and answer 4 to `Proves it:`. Mechanical fixes, docs changes and known-cause bug fixes skip it. Tests pin the step, and `make check` and `jgauge test-slot` pass. `templates/brief.md`, the principle, `skills/deeper/` and the parser are not to be touched.

### Reviewers
- Reviewer A: 6 findings
- Reviewer B: 7 findings
- The two reviewers agreed on the three central problems:
  - the `Instruments:`/`Read:` contradiction
  - the step keying on the playbook name rather than the kind of work
  - the hard-coded playbook list

  They differed mostly on severity, and B added three small points.

### Act On

**1. The step writes lines the brief template forbids or never defines (A1, B1).**
- `templates/brief.md:17` tells the home to leave `Read:` out of its own briefs.
- `Instruments:` exists nowhere outside this diff.
- The template is under "Do not touch", so the PR cannot settle the conflict there.
- The fix belongs in the step: send answer 3 to a line the template already has, such as the task body or the Done-when list, and record any template follow-up in the Result.
- As written, a home that reads the template, which it is told to do first, gets the opposite instruction.

**2. The step keys on the playbook name, not the kind of work (A2, B2, A4, B3).**
- `bug-fix` always skips, although its playbook covers bugs whose cause is unknown. The intent's boundary exempts only a known cause.
- Outcome work run under `feature` or `autonomous-run` always skips.
- The hand-kept list of ten names drifts silently when playbooks are added.
- The test locks the `bug-fix` mismatch in by labelling it "known bug".
- One fix covers all of it: take the kind of work as the input in every case. The name list and its drift problem then disappear. This is the code-judo move the scope asks for.

**3. For a scout request, the scout's playbook decides the step (A3).**
- Both scout playbooks are in the deeper arm, so every request runs the four questions. That includes requests whose Deliver asks for a docs brief or a known-cause bug-fix brief.
- This breaks the second Done-when line for briefs written by scouts.

- **Prose-only skip (B6).** The extra skip, for a task whose Done-when already names its data, instruments and judge, is a prose override after the block has printed `deeper`. It should be one more input kind. That falls out naturally from finding 2's fix.

### Noted
- **A6:** The test compares named lines against the template. It is a symptom of finding 1. Once answer 3 goes to an existing line, the gap closes. A pin can be added with that fix if wanted.
- **B7:** No evidence of `make check` or `jgauge test-slot` in the diff. The merge gate runs these, and the Result must report them. This is not a code finding.

None.

### Intent
> Run the Proves it, Size, Playbook and required-field checks at `jbus queue add`, so an incomplete brief is refused before the user ever sees it, with the launch keeping its checks as a backstop. Bind an approval to a deterministic meaning fingerprint over the scope and risk fields, so typos, formatting, reordering and Task-only edits keep the go, while any added or changed Done-when line, path, number or value re-asks. Record both the fingerprint and the full `brief_sha`, print them for other bots to verify, keep old full-sha rows working, and document the method and its known limit.

### Reviewers
- Reviewer A: 9 findings
- Reviewer B: 8 findings
- They agreed on four findings independently: template text passing `_filled`, negation keeping the go, the two separate check lists, and the CLI's string matching. The review skill's questions were asked.

### Act On
- **Template text passes `queue add` for Task, Done when, Pull request and Review.** Raised by A1 and B1.
  - A brief copied straight from `templates/brief.md` passes those four fields, so it is queued and put to the user.
  - This breaks the core Done-when line: "refuses an incomplete brief".
  - The cause is concrete. `_filled` only checks for a leading `<`, while `_template` already exists and handles both `<` and `|`.
  - The existing test hides the gap by writing `Task: <the request>` without the template's quotes.
- **Negation by contraction keeps the go, and the stated limit does not mention it.** Raised by A3 and B2.
  - Stripping the apostrophe is the author's choice, not the spec's. It turns `shouldn't` into a two-edit typo of `should`, so a Done-when line that flips its meaning keeps the approval.
  - That defeats "still catching real changes to intent".
  - Opposite words within two edits (`include`/`exclude`) and swapped direction after filler-dropping and sorting come from the spec itself. They must still be stated in the limit section, which the Done-when list requires.
  - The approval is the user's authorisation, so this carries a risk tag.
- **The add-time checks and the launch-time checks are two hand-kept lists.** Raised by A4 and B3.
  - The task exists because checks ran in the wrong place. Keeping `faults` and `CHECKS`/`ASKED` in step by docstring is a rule in prose that will drift.
  - Fix: keep one tuple in `jbriefs.parse`, which `faults` runs and dispatch reads. That makes the launch a backstop by construction.
  - Both files are in Where.

### Consider
- **The home skill discards `its go does not hold` on a successful add.** Raised by A2.
  - The user is still asked again later, through the launch gate, so the intent is not broken.
  - But the home learns of the voided go a pass late. Printing it is a two-line fix in a file inside Where.
- **The approval record's `scope` field is never checked against anything.** Raised by A5.
  - `scope` and `holds` can disagree after a typo fix, and a bot comparing `scope` hashes would refuse a brief that jbus launches.
  - The record has no version for the fingerprint method.
  - The hand-edit route to widening a go is mostly hypothetical, since editing `queue.json` by hand is out of bounds.
  - The docs should at least say that `scope` equality is stricter than `holds`.
- **The CLI picks its output by matching the end of a string.** Raised by A6 and B5. It is fragile and cheap to fix by returning the state as data.
- **The PR description says the launch checks are unchanged.** Raised by A8.
  - The playbook check is now stricter, so some approved rows that used to launch now gate.
  - The change is intended by the task; the description should say so.
- **`approve` does not run `faults`.** Raised by B4.
  - Old incomplete rows can still be put to the user, and the launch backstop catches them later.
  - The fix is a one-line check.

### Noted
- A7: redundant calls (`designed` run twice, a `_filled` result discarded, a second ROUTING strip). These are subsumed by the single-tuple fix.
- A9: re-prioritising an old, incomplete row would cost its go. This is theoretical, since every row queued today is complete.
- B6: greedy pairing in `_pairs` errs only toward asking again, which is safe.

### Dismissed
- B7: `asks.py` is outside the Where line. The Where line named the CLI layer, and the queue verbs live in `asks.py`. That is missing context, not a stray edit.
- B8: the PR description could not be confirmed. The reviewer lacked the description. The concrete gap in the limit section is already carried by A3/B2.

## Lead judgment

Nine distinct issues came in from the two readings. After merging duplicates, three are **Act on**, one is **Consider**, one is **Noted** and three are **Dismissed**.

**Merges**
- **Concurrent snapshots (A1 + B1):** both readings found that `take` has no lock and now runs from many homes as well as the timer. B1's other two points, mixed-content commits and two homes' edits landing in one commit, are folded into A3.
- **Restore command empties the file (A2 + B2):** the same finding.
- **Handoff gains a duty to write rules (A5 + B3):** the same finding. A5 rated it `warning` and B3 rated it `nit`; I keep `warning`.
- **`docs/jbus.md` outside the Where line (A6 + B4):** the same finding.

**Act on**
- **Concurrent snapshots.** Before this change, only the timer ran `take`, twice a day. Now any home's edit to `standing.md` runs it too, so overlapping runs will happen, and both failure paths are concrete:
  - **False alarm:** a collision on `index.lock` fails the timer's unit, and its `OnFailure` alarm then alerts the desk and every project.
  - **Lost commit:** another run's `git reset` between `add` and `diff --cached` leaves an edit with no commit. That breaks the main Done-when line.
  - The fix is a `flock` inside `snapshot.py`, which is within the Where line.
- **Restore command.** The documented restore truncates the live `standing.md` before `git show` can fail. It will fail in an ordinary case: undoing a repo's first rule, where `<commit>^` has no `standing.md`. The test never runs that case. This is a data-loss path in a document whose whole purpose is recovery.
- **Handoff duty.** The handoff skill now gains a duty to write rules, which the task did not ask for. It also contradicts the sentence just before it. Cutting it is cheap.

**Consider**
- **Mixed-content commits (A3, with B1's commit-contents points).** The commit named by `--why` still sweeps in the whole tree.
  - The Done-when checks still hold. The undo path is path-limited, and "own commit" is read through `log -- <repo>/standing.md`.
  - The real cost is that unscoped `git log` messages misdescribe their commits. In rare cases, an undo also reverts a second home's rule on the same file.
  - Path-scoping `--why` commits is worth doing, but it is a design widening, not a blocker.

**Noted**
- **`docs/jbus.md` (A6/B4).** It is outside the Where line, but documenting a new flag on the command page is correct and expected.

**Dismissed**
- **A4:** the brief chose a skill step ("Design: one flag and one step") and named all three skill files. A durable verb is out of scope and the reading itself says so. The wording drift in handoff disappears with the handoff fix above.
- **A7:** a test helper is not a legacy API. Migrating the inline copies would mean editing tests this PR did not change.
- **B5:** the test name is a nitpick.

An unedited `templates/brief.md` is not refused on those four fields, which misses "an incomplete brief can't be queued", and docs/jbus.md and the home skill claim otherwise. > Add a `Proves it:` line to `templates/brief.md`, right after `Done when:`. The brief parser and jbus's pre-launch check accept it only when it names something outside the agent (a test, a metric, a dataset, an external judge or the user). They refuse empty, template, self-referential and review-only answers with a one-line reason. Missing lines are grandfathered or refused without stranding an approved row, and the change is tested and documented.

- Reviewer A: 7 findings
- Reviewer B: 6 findings
- The two agreed on every substantive issue. A alone raised the grandfathering scope (A2) and the double gate (A3).

  - "make sure the reviewer is happy"
  - "self-test"
  - "`the crewmate` checks it"
  - "the reviewer is 100% sure"
  - "the model is the judge"

  `proof()` returns on the first `_OUTSIDE` match, and `_ready` launches whenever `proven()` is empty. So this is the gate failing at the exact refusal the task names. The tests pin only the accepting side of the precedence rule. I rate it `error`: it defeats the line's purpose. Note that the readers' line numbers for `parse.py` differ (A has `_OUTSIDE` at 31, B has it at 133), so the crewmate should locate it by name.

### Intent
> Ship /deeper (sections 1, 2, 5 and 6 of the design): a manual skill that returns the four answers and a rewritten prompt, a non-blocking gate when a home runs it, the 25th principle `depth-over-breadth`, the `jdrift` source entry, the credit in `THIRD_PARTY.md`, and a rerunnable blind eval in `evals/deeper/` whose committed Result says honestly whether /deeper won. "If it did not, say so: that is a finding, not a reason to tune the eval."

### Reviewers
- Reviewer A: 5 findings (3 warning, 2 nit)
- Reviewer B: 8 findings (4 warning, 4 nit)
- Both readers raised two findings independently: raw sources have no control for the skill's own list (A2/B2), and `write()` wipes the committed runs before any call (A3/B3). Neither reader reported a missed "Done when" line in the skill, the principle, jdrift or the credit. The eval's evidence is where the weight sits.

### Act On
1. **The verdict "won" rests on one run of two** (B1, built on A1). Run 1 lost under the rule. The only change before run 2 was the rewrite's output format (fence to block quote). In 8 of 10 cases the "outside" measure flipped sign between the two runs. The README says only what both runs agree on is a finding, and then calls the eval won on run 2 alone. This is the move the brief warned against, and the Result is the "Proves it" of this pull request.
2. **The "outside" measure counts any backtick span** (A1). A rescored the committed briefs: without the backtick branch, the two arms are level (0.34 vs 0.33). The rise from plain to deeper on outside is formatting, because the skill tells writers to name things by path. Together with item 1, this means the eval shows nothing on proof outside the agent. Fixing the measure makes it stricter, not more favourable, so it is not tuning. The Result must then say that outside was not shown.
3. **Raw sources have no control for copying the skill's list** (A2+B2, consensus). Seven of the twelve `RAW` kinds are the words of question 2 of the skill. Yet the README claims the effect holds "not only by copying the skill's own examples". A `beyond` count for raw needs no model calls. Otherwise, narrow the claim to instruments.

First, I find every use of `Task` (Grep for `Task`, `status`, `doneAt`) so I know what the compiler will need to re-check.
I'm following the opening rule, "Make the compiler reject impossible states... unhandled variants": the current shape allows `status: 'open'` with a `doneAt` set, and adding `cancelledAt?` on top would make that worse.
So I replace the type with a discriminated union in which each timestamp exists only on its own variant:
`type Task = { status: 'open' } | { status: 'done'; doneAt: Date } | { status: 'cancelled'; cancelledAt: Date };`
Then I add `const _exhaustive: never = task;` in the `default` branch of each `switch (task.status)`, so any variant left unhandled becomes a compile error.
If tasks come from JSON or the DB, I update the boundary parse function so it builds these variants instead of casting.

## Lead judgment

### Intent
> Every gate is act-unless-stopped: the thread acts on its default at once, and a plain open question closes by silence after 2 hours. A gate whose default deletes data, rewrites history, spends money, touches prod or real users, changes access or secrets, or publishes must carry `Holds:` and a `Fail-safe:`. Such a gate waits for the user's answer and is never closed by silence. `jbus gate` refuses a gate with no default, one whose recommended option is not the default, and a `Holds:` gate with no fail-safe. The rule, the definition and the table ship in the skills, the template and the docs, in this one pull request.

### Reviewers
- Reviewer A: 6 findings
- Reviewer B: 6 findings
- They agreed on two things: the "acted on" and fail-safe state never reaches anything the user reads, and the doubled `(default, recommended)` mark is redundant. Neither raised the other's critical finding.
- I had no checkout to trace these against. Each judgment rests on the evidence the reader gave, and each critical finding names a concrete path through unchanged lines that the new state now reaches.

### Act On
- **A1 · Re-piping a silence-closed gate with `Holds:` is answered "already answered".** Raised by A. `ask` still treats any answered record as settled, and an answer by silence now counts as one. Suppose a thread first gates plainly, then finds the default deletes data and re-pipes with `Holds: deletes data`. The new lines are thrown away and the thread is told to go by an answer nobody gave. That is the one outcome the fail-safe exists to prevent, so it is a real `error` on the data path.
- **B1 · A `Holds:` gate answered with its default never reaches its thread.** Raised by B. `tell` and the page skip any `keeps` answer, because before this change the default had always been carried out already. A held gate has not been carried out. So the user's "yes, the recommended default" does nothing, and the held action parks for good. Only a differing answer moves it. This breaks the "waits for the user's answer" line, and docs/jbus.md:132 now says something false. The failure keeps work parked rather than destroying anything, so it gets no risk tag. It is still an `error`.
- **A2 · Silence closes the link-conflict questions that ask the home.** Raised by A. The home's reader selects `.answer == null`. Once `silent` fills the answer, the rebase line is never sent and the stack link sits. This is a concrete path, and it does the reverse of "no question parks work".
- **A4 + B2 · "Shown as already acted on" and "with the dry-run, plan or bundle attached" are not met.** Raised by both. `acted`, `holds` and `fail_safe` reach only `waiting-on-user.json`. The item's `line`, the home's jq block (skills/home/SKILL.md, inside Where) and the page do not show them. The only test reads the JSON file, which is a proxy for what the user sees. The `line` and the home's jq/printf are inside Where and are the fix for this PR. The page panel and `waiting._blocks` are noted for later.

### Consider
- **A6 · skills/home/SKILL.md:822 still says "only their name closes a question".** Raised by A. This file is one the Done when line requires to state the rule, and it now contradicts it. The fix is cheap and inside Where.
- **A5 + B5 · Both marks are required though they can never differ.** Raised by both. Treating `(default)` as the pick, and refusing `(recommended)` on any other option, meets the Done when line just as well. It removes two refusal branches and stops the outright refusal of gates in the old `(default)` form. The current form is not wrong, so this is the user's call.
- **A3 · The words panel renders a close by silence as "Your answer".** Raised by A. `basis()` is right, but the user's own record misattributes the answer to them. The panel is outside Where, so this needs a follow-up row.
- **B3 · Expert findings now recommend doing nothing and dismiss themselves after 2 hours.** Raised by B. The test fixture was bent to pass instead of the expert skill being decided. That runs against what the user wanted (no lost work), but skills/expert/SKILL.md is outside Where, so it needs a follow-up row.

### Intent
> Answer P7's two questions from the code. First, does jmerge's "fails over today's main" check run on the merge result? If not, make it go stale when main changed a caller or a dependency of the PR's files (or a lockfile), with a test. Second, does a T3 launch take an effort setting? Answer from T3's own schema, record the decision in THIRD_PARTY.md, and never raise effort above medium. `make check` and `jgauge test-slot -- make check` must pass.

### Reviewers
- Reviewer A: 7 findings (4 warning, 3 nit)
- Reviewer B: 5 findings (4 warning, 1 nit)
- They agreed on two findings independently: the unproven effort shape (A1 = B4) and bare-name test imports (A4 = B2). They also agreed on the cost of parsing and subprocesses (A6 ≈ B5).
- Their line numbers for the same functions differ. For `modules`, A gives ready.py:210 and B gives :868. For `related`, A gives cli.py:169 and B gives :659. One reviewer likely cited hunk-relative lines. I have no checkout to verify, so I give B's numbers below, since they agree with B's other anchors (:926, :941). The crewmate should confirm them.

### Act On
1. **The effort shape is not proven (A1, B4).** The repo's T3 schema types `options` as `anyOf [{}, null]`, so the shape `[{"id":"effort","value":…}]` is asserted, not read from T3. The validation test passes whatever jroles prints. "Done when" asks for the answer "read from T3's own tool schema", and "Proves it" asks for that schema to be quoted. Neither is met. If the shape is wrong, every Claude role silently launches at `high`, which breaks the user's hard rule. Two reviewers raised it independently.
2. **Codex and Grok lines are unchecked against the medium cap (A2).** THIRD_PARTY.md and the docstring claim the rule holds "for every role the map names". By the PR's own reasoning, though, a line that sends no effort gets the provider's default, and nobody checked those defaults. The fix is cheap: narrow the claim to Claude lines and gate the Codex/Grok question.
3. **The rename path is missed (B1).** `related` builds `ours` from `one.files`, but GitHub lists only the new path of a rename. A caller that main adds under the old module name is never matched. This is a concrete execution path and the heart of #613. The fix is small: pass `left` in.
4. **The check fails open when the head is unreadable (A3).** If `git show <head>:<path>` fails, `ours` is empty, so no dependency can be found and the stale green stands. Every other git failure in jmerge blocks the merge. This is a merge gate, so failing open is the wrong default.
5. **Bare-name sibling imports are missed (A4, B2).** At least ten test files import siblings by bare name, including this PR's own `tests/test_jmerge_callers.py`. The task's "dependency changed" case is therefore missed in this very repo. Two reviewers raised it independently.

### Consider
- **Path mentions in prose count as dependencies (B3).** Docs that name paths go stale whenever those paths change, and this PR itself is such a case. The check fails closed, so this is noise, not a wrong merge, but for a guarded PR it means a forced rebase. Restricting matches to executable files is the tradeoff.
- **Docs edited outside "Where" (A7).** The edits to docs/configuration.md, docs/jmerge.md and docs/jroles.md each describe the new behaviour, so they are probably right to keep. Whoever wrote the "Where" line should confirm that.

### Noted
- **Substring and conftest-suffix matching (A5).** It fails closed and only adds noise.
- **One subprocess and one parse per pair of files (A6, B5).** This is premature until a run actually nears the 300 s limit.

None.

# Lead Judgment: P6, the cap on rebases after fixed

### Intent
> Once a crewmate has written `fixed and green`, a third rebase forced by main is not made. The crewmate writes one stop line in its Result and pipes a gate, and jbus surfaces the pull request as waiting. The count is kept where jbus or jmerge can read it, and a test drives three rebases and finds the stop on the third. How a rebase is pushed does not change.

### Reviewers
- Reviewer A: 6 findings (3 warning, 3 nit)
- Reviewer B: 5 findings (4 warning, 1 nit)
- Both independently found the jbus step mapping, the `Fixed:` proxy and the gap in jmerge test coverage.
- I could not check line numbers against the repo, because this workspace is not a checkout. A and B give different SKILL.md lines for the same block (A: 62–87, B: 379–443). I keep each reviewer's own line, and the merged findings use B's.

### Act On
1. **The held pull request shows as waiting on its crewmate** (A1, B1). `held a third rebase` maps to the `rebase` step, which is owned by the crew. Once the gate is answered, or if it is never parked, the row reads "Rebase, its crewmate" indefinitely, but only the user can lift the hold. This is the "jbus surfaces it as waiting" Done-when line, met with the wrong owner, and the test table locks it in. The repo already routes reasons only the user can clear to `hold`. Both reviewers raised it, so I take it as a consensus finding.
2. **Running the block again on a held head tells the crew to park another gate** (A3). The block prints `hold:` on every run and the prose says to park a gate on `hold`. `mainmoved` wakes every red pull request once per main commit, and a held pull request is often red, so gates pile up. This is the "run twice" case, on a concrete path.
3. **The count spans the whole brief, not the last Result** (B2). SKILL.md says every block reads the last result. A follow-up round inherits the old `Rebased after fixed:` lines, so its first conflict is held at once. The path is concrete and the fix is small: reset the counters on `## Result`.

### Consider
- **The cap starts at `Fixed:`, not at "fixed and green"** (A2, B3). This is a real proxy for the Done-when wording. However, the PR states the choice (`fixed and green` is a message, not a line in the brief), and the error runs in the safe direction: it holds sooner, behind a gate to the user. Adding a "green" marker to the brief is a design call. Either do it or record the deviation in the Result.
- **The test does not run jmerge's `waits()` or the stopped-rebase count** (A5, B4). The Done-when test is met: three rebases are driven and the third is stopped. The ordering in `cli.py:703` and the `counted` call in the conflict branch can still be deleted without any test failing. Both are worth one more assertion each.
- **The hold is recorded at the local HEAD, not at the pushed head** (A4). This needs a refused push followed by another move of main. The block already has `pushed`, so the fix is one word.
- **The once-per-head check accepts any earlier hold line at that head** (B5). The scenario is narrow (lift, then a stopped rebase, then an abort back to X). The fix for A3, which compares against the last hold-or-lift line, closes this too.

### Noted
- A6: the test helper's `home` argument also switches the slug. This is valid, but it affects one caller and is test-only.

### Dismissed
None.

### Agreement Map
The reviewers agreed on three things: the mapping, the proxy and the coverage gap. Two of these sit squarely on Done-when lines, which is a strong signal. They diverged on state over time. A saw the problem when the same head is seen again (A3, A4), and B saw it across rounds and lifts (B2, B5). Neither covered the other's ground. Taken together, they show that the block's reading of the brief's history is the weakest part of the change.

### Intent

The exceptions are gates whose default deletes data, rewrites history, spends money, touches prod or real users, changes access or secrets, or publishes. Each of those must carry `Holds: <case>` and a `Fail-safe:` line, and it waits for the user, never closed by silence. `jbus gate` refuses a gate with no default, a default that is not the recommended option, a `Holds:` gate with no fail-safe, and an unknown case. First, I don't add `'cancelled'` to the union with an optional `cancelledAt`. That would make states like "done without doneAt" or "open with cancelledAt" possible to represent.
I follow the first sentence of the principle: "Make the compiler reject impossible states… make illegal states unrepresentable." So I reshape `Task` into a discriminated union where each state carries exactly its own timestamp:
`type Task = { status: 'open' } | { status: 'done'; doneAt: Date } | { status: 'cancelled'; cancelledAt: Date };`
Then I run `tsc --noEmit` and fix every site it flags. Any `switch (task.status)` gets a `default: { const _exhaustive: never = task; }` check so a missed variant fails at compile time.
If `Task` comes from a schema (DB migration, OpenAPI), I add the state there and regenerate the type rather than editing it by hand.

First I replace the `as Order` cast, because it's an unchecked assertion on external data. I'm following the "External data is untyped until parsed" bullet: add a parse function at the RPC boundary.
If an authoritative schema already owns `Order` (OpenAPI, protobuf, a zod schema), I derive from it ("Derive types from authoritative schemas") and don't hand-roll a new one.
The line I write: `const order = parseOrder(JSON.parse(body) as unknown);`, where `parseOrder(x: unknown): Order` checks `items` is an array, or does `OrderSchema.parse(...)` with zod.
Invalid input then fails at the boundary with a 400, not as a `TypeError` on `order.items.length` later.
Downstream code trusts the `Order` type, and ID fields get branded types (`OrderId`) set at parse time.

### Intent

One run's git reset can also wipe another's staged edit, so that edit never gets its own commit. Hold an exclusive flock in .git across add, commit and push; the callers are skills/home/SKILL.md:79, skills/home/scoped-homes.md:7 and skills/handoff/SKILL.md:92 (principle: foundational-thinking) (bucket: Act on) (risk: concurrency)`

A mistyped hash, a root commit, or the commit that created standing.md leaves the rules file empty, and the doc's next step snapshots that empty file. Document a form that writes only on success (git restore --source=<commit>^ -- <repo>/standing.md, or a temp file followed by mv), say what to do when the bad edit created the file, and add a test for that case (principle: prove-it-works) (bucket: Act on) (risk: data)`

They refuse an empty line, the template's own text, and any proof by the crew, crewmate, reviewer, agent, "self", "the model" or a review alone, giving one line saying why. A brief without the line is grandfathered or refused so that no approved row is stranded. Tests cover each kind, and the home skill and `docs/` name the new line.

### Reviewers
- Reviewer A: 7 findings
- Reviewer B: 6 findings
- The two agreed on every theme. They differed only in severity, and in the line numbers they gave for `parse.py`: A puts `_OUTSIDE` at 31-36 and `proof()` at 126-128, B puts them at 133-142 and 190-192. I could not settle this from here, so the lines below follow B where the two conflict, and the function names are the reliable anchor.

### Act On

**1. `_OUTSIDE` is matched first and is loose enough to accept the agent's own word** (A1, B1, B2)
Both reviewers found this independently and gave concrete inputs that pass. "the crewmate will make sure it works" matches `make \w`. ``the `reviewer` says so`` matches any backticked text. "the reviewer is 100% sure" matches `%`. "the model is the judge" matches `judge`. "self-test" matches `\btest\b`. "the reviewer gives his word" matches `his word`. I rate it `error`, not A's `warning`, because it defeats the feature's one purpose.

`proven()` returns `""` whenever `proves_it` returns None. Nothing ties that exemption to the time of approval or to the brief sha, so a new brief that leaves the line out launches with no gate.
